cards.headline: The Solar System is mostly empty
lines: Shrink the Sun to a 1-metre ball, and Earth is a 9 mm marble about 107 m away.
Neptune would be over 3 km away.
The nearest other star would be about 29,000 km away.

visual.caption: Distance from a 1 m Sun, to scale

cards.source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheets; scale computed from mean distances and the Sun's diameter.

cards.headline: Seasons come from Earth's tilt
lines: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4°.
When your hemisphere leans toward the Sun, longer days and more direct sunlight bring summer.
It isn't distance: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
cards.source: NASA Space Place, 'What Causes the Seasons?'; Chaisson & McMillan, 'Astronomy Today'.

cards.headline: Why the Moon has phases
lines: The Sun always lights half of the Moon.
As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half.
One full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.
cards.source: NASA Science, 'Moon Phases'; Chaisson & McMillan, 'Astronomy Today'.

cards.headline: A light-year is a distance, not a time
lines: It's how far light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion km.
The nearest star beyond the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.
So looking far into space means looking back in time.

cards.headline: Stars forge the elements
lines: Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.
Massive stars build heavier elements, and their explosions scatter them through space.
The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made in earlier stars.
cards.source: Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler & Hoyle (1957), Reviews of Modern Physics; NASA.

cards.question: Which is the largest planet in our Solar System?
cards.why: Jupiter — more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined.

cards.question: In which year did humans first walk on the Moon?
cards.why: Apollo 11, 20 July 1969. 1957 was Sputnik; 1961 was Yuri Gagarin's first human spaceflight.
cards.source: NASA History Office, Apollo 11 mission overview.

cards.question: Which planet is the hottest?
cards.why: Venus, at about 465 °C: its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

cards.question: What mainly causes Earth's seasons?
cards.why: The roughly 23.4° tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere through the year.
cards.source: NASA Space Place, 'What Causes the Seasons?'.

cards.question: Roughly how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
cards.why: About 8 minutes 20 seconds to cross roughly 150 million km.

cards.headline: Venus spins slower than it orbits
cards.text: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once but about 225 days to orbit — and it spins backwards. (Sunrise to sunrise takes about 117 days.)

cards.headline: Moon footprints could last millions of years
cards.text: With no wind or rain, almost nothing erodes them. Only tiny meteorite impacts slowly churn the surface.
cards.source: NASA, Apollo lunar surface science summaries.

cards.headline: The ISS circles Earth about every 90 minutes
cards.text: Travelling at about 28,000 km/h, its crew sees roughly 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.

visual.caption: sunrises a day aboard the ISS

cards.source: NASA, International Space Station facts and figures.

cards.headline: A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh about a billion tonnes
cards.text: Neutron stars pack more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 km across.
cards.source: NASA Goddard, 'Neutron Stars'; Chaisson & McMillan, 'Astronomy Today'.

cards.headline: What is a black hole?

steps.headline: 1 · Too much in too little
lines: When a very massive star collapses, its core can shrink without limit.
Gravity becomes so strong that nothing — not even light — can escape.

steps.headline: 2 · The event horizon
lines: The boundary of no return is called the event horizon.
Well outside it, things can orbit safely, as planets orbit the Sun.

steps.headline: 3 · Giants at the centre
lines: Most large galaxies have a supermassive black hole at their core.
Ours, Sagittarius A*, is about 4 million times the Sun's mass.

steps.headline: 4 · Seeing the unseeable
lines: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadow of the black hole in galaxy M87.
In 2022 it released an image of Sagittarius A*.

cards.source: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2019, 2022), Astrophysical Journal Letters; Nobel Prize in Physics 2020.

cards.headline: Space: the takeaways
points: The Solar System is mostly empty space.
Tilt, not distance, makes the seasons.
Phases: how much of the lit half we see.
Your atoms were forged in stars.
